To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
• We propose a runtime system that automatically schedules legacy kernels on heterogeneous architectures with distributed memory.

(a) we can achieve performance improvements of up to 4.4x for applications that use the kernels in the Intel MKL library, (b) we can achieve up to 3.4x improvement for a set of applications that use kernels in the Intel TBB library, and (c) we can achieve an overall performance improvement of 2.5x for a set of real applications that use the Intel MKL, Intel TBB, and OpenBLAS libraries.

(1) We present the first runtime that enables transparently executing legacy code on heterogeneous platforms with non-coherent interconnections, (2) we show that our runtime achieves speedup of up to 2.7x over CPU-only execution on the SPEC CPU 2006 benchmarks, and (3) we demonstrate that our runtime achieves a performance improvement of up to 3.2x over a state-of-the-art runtime for the same benchmarks on the same hardware.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following question: How can a runtime system transparently schedule kernels on heterogeneous platforms and manage data placement in order to maximize performance while minimizing programming effort?
(a) the automatic detection of computational kernels, (b) the automatic scheduling of kernels on CPU or GPU, and (c) the transparent data placement between CPU and GPU.
the following questions: (1) What are the performance implications of scheduling kernels on the CPU and GPU?
